retrieved.title: CrashLoopBackOff
retrieved.text:
## Symptoms

- `kubectl get pods` shows `STATUS` as `CrashLoopBackOff` or `Error` with a climbing restart count.
- The pod phase may still be `Running` because a container is mid-backoff, not because the app is healthy.
- Current logs are often empty or just a short "waiting" message. The useful signal is usually in the **previous** container logs (`kubectl logs --previous`).
- Events include `BackOff`, `Failed`, or `Unhealthy` from the kubelet.

retrieved.title: CrashLoopBackOff
retrieved.text:
# CrashLoopBackOff

A pod is in `CrashLoopBackOff` when Kubernetes has started the container repeatedly and it keeps exiting. The kubelet backs off between restarts, so the pod can sit in this state for a long time while the application itself only lives for a few seconds at a time.

retrieved.title: CPU throttling
retrieved.text:
## Diagnosis

1. Read the requests and limits:

   ```bash
   kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources}'
   ```

2. Compare usage with the limit:

   ```bash
   kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> --containers
   ```

3. Check throttling in Prometheus:

   ```promql
   sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{namespace="<ns>", pod="<pod>"}[5m]))
     / sum by (container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_periods_total{namespace="<ns>", pod="<pod>"}[5m]))
   ```

4. If a rollout changed the resources, compare revisions with `kubectl rollout history deploy/<name> -n <ns> --revision=<n>`.

retrieved.title: CrashLoopBackOff
retrieved.text:
## Diagnosis

1. Read the last termination reason and exit code:

   ```bash
   kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>
   kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{range .status.containerStatuses[*]}{.name}{" "}{.state}{" "}{.lastState.terminated}{"\n"}{end}'
   ```

2. Always fetch previous logs if `restartCount > 0`:

   ```bash
   kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --previous --tail=200
   kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> --tail=200
   ```

3. Confirm the command that actually ran (`command` / `args` in the pod spec) and whether the image entrypoint expects different arguments.
4. If logs mention a missing file, env var, or connection refused, inspect the related ConfigMap, Secret, and Service.

retrieved.title: CPU throttling
retrieved.text:
## Fixes

- Raise the CPU `limit` (or remove it and rely on `requests` for scheduling) to a value measured from real usage plus headroom.
- If a recent rollout lowered the limit and the pod is now throttled, the rollout caused a regression, even though the pod is `Running` and `Ready` with no restarts. Roll back to the previous revision, which restores the limit, then fix the manifest. "No crash" does not mean "no incident": slower work is the failure.
- Scale out (more replicas) when the work can be spread across pods; this does not make a single slow request faster.
- Size runtime thread pools to the cgroup quota (`GOMAXPROCS`, `-XX:ActiveProcessorCount`, worker counts).
- Raise probe `timeoutSeconds` if probes fail only because the container is throttled.
